articles.title: GOP 'clash' on tap as Jim Jordan makes plans to disrupt House leadership: report
articles.description: Whether or not the Republican Party remains in control of the House after the midterms, a battle for the chamber’s leadership is already shaping up. According to a report from CNN, Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) is quietly laying the groundwork to run for House GOP leader if Republicans lose the chamber in November, setting up a potential "clash" with Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA). CNN reported that half a dozen lawmakers and aides believe Jordan, the House Judiciary chair, is preparing a bid. Publicly, Jordan says he is solely focused on helping Republicans keep the majority and supporting Johnson as speaker, and his allies insist he is a team player who isn’t trying to undercut him. According to the report, "In a private conversation with one Republican lawmaker, Jordan said he would have kept lawmakers in Washington longer to hold more votes that would be politically challenging for Democrats. He also expressed interest in holding more votes on President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill that has been blocked in the Republican-led Senate, arguing that would help House Republicans on the campaign trail even if the bill won’t be signed into law." “Jim has a different vision on how he would have gone about this,” the source told CNN. “He clearly wants to be minority leader,” a senior GOP aide also told CNN. “He is fully running. He is calling candidates.” Johnson has said he will stay on as GOP leader whether Republicans win or lose the House. “I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government,” he said, according to CNN. Jordan allies have argued to some in Trump’s orbit that he is "uniquely positioned" to defend the president against Democratic investigations, pointing to his experience leading Judiciary and defending Trump during both impeachments, two sources told CNN. CNN also reported that through September Jordan donated $1.97 million directly to candidates and $2.65 million to the party’s House campaign arm, according to a source familiar with the matter. He has traveled to 33 states this cycle and this week launched a 19-day campaign swing from Washington to Florida. Jordan ran for speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy’s ouster but faced opposition from moderate Republicans who felt he was too much of a conservative firebrand, CNN reported. Since then, it said, he has worked to "mend relationships," including with lawmakers who said "Jordan’s allies threatened them physically or verbally," by campaigning in their districts and donating to their campaigns.

articles.title: Afghanistan | AWD Preparedness and Response Plan 2026 2027
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Background In 2026, an estimated 21.9 million people, around 45% of Afghanistan’s population, will require humanitarian assistance, reflecting only a slight decrease from 2025 and keeping Afghanistan among the world’s largest humanitarian crises. This includes 17.4 million people facing acute food insecurity, of whom 4.7 million are in Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC ) Phase 4 (Emergency), more than double last year›s figure. Children and women remain highly vulnerable, with malnutrition worsening due to severe food insecurity. Reference to Afghanistan National health policy, Afghanistan has an area of 652,864 square kilometers, and as of 1403 (2024) in the Islamic calendar, its population is estimated to be 35.7 million people. Of this, 18.2 million (51.0%) are male, and 17.5 million (49.0%) are female. The population is estimated 48 millions as per UN estimation. Afghanistan has 34 provinces and 401 districts with monotonous geography and scattered population with many hard to reach areas. Humanitarian needs continue to be driven by deep structural vulnerabilities and recurrent shocks. Drought conditions persist, severely affecting 12 provinces and impacting 3.4 million people, compounded by a forecasted La Niña pattern bringing below‑average rainfall and rising temperatures. Afghanistan also continues to face frequent earthquakes, floods, disease outbreaks, and large-scale returnee inflows, with more than 2.61 million Afghans returning from Pakistan and Iran in 2025 alone, placing immense pressure on host communities and overstretched basic services. Protection risks especially for women and girls remain severe and are expected to intensify due to enforced restrictions by the de facto authorities, alongside explosive ordnance contamination, child labour, early marriage, and gender based violence. On average, 50 people are killed or injured each month due to explosive ordnance. Compounding these issues, Afghanistan’s economy continues to shrink, household debt is widespread, and livelihood opportunities remain limited, further eroding community resilience and deepening humanitarian dependence. The massive returnee influx further strains basic services, shelter, WASH systems, and health facilities, especially in border and rural areas. Amid these challenges, the WASH and Health Clusters remain committed to delivering essential services, including safe water, sanitation, hygiene promotion, primary healthcare, disease outbreak response, and nutrition services. Efforts prioritize the most vulnerable communities, focusing on life‑saving and protective interventions and ensuring equitable access across the most severely affected regions.

articles.title: “Demonic Stuff”: Kansas GOP Accuses Democrat of Being a Witch
articles.description: Witch hunts are back in vogue with Kansas Republicans—literally. Ty Masterson, the Republican candidate in the Kansas gubernatorial race, accused his Democratic opponent, Cindy Holscher, of being an actual witch capable of “demonic” magic, while speaking at the Praise Chapel in Wichita on Sunday. Masterson introduced the dubious portion of his pseudo-sermon by suggesting that God wanted him to run for Kansas’s top political office. “God’s armies are out there in this,” Masterson said. “What we’re fighting right now is a spiritual battle that I’ve never seen before, in [this] state, in this politics. “Evil is maturing with the brotherhood, and it is rising to a level that is just in your face,” Masterson continued as a pianist played a contemplative melody beside him. “Really, my race and the U.S. Senate race with Roger Marshall versus [Adam] Hamilton. Those are spiritual battles. “Like I said, my opponent, she didn’t even hide it,” Masterson added. “She talked—they had witch—I mean, they’re doing like witchcraft spells on TikTok so she can win the governorship. I mean, they’re like … it’s like demonic stuff that they’re doing, right? Just in your face that way.” The state senator had seemingly drawn his conclusions from a series of playful TikTok videos posted by Holscher’s 20-year-old daughter, Maddie, who had shared clips of her and her mom brushing their teeth set to a song from the Wicked soundtrack. “Casting a spell so my mom wins Kansas Governor except she’s so done with me,” Maddie Holscher captioned one clip from April, in which she waves her arms around her mother. The unserious memes offered voters a fun porthole into the Democratic candidate’s family life. In May, Holscher said that the “goofy” videos her daughter makes “mean a lot” to her, and encouraged people to check them out. The younger Holscher responded to the Republican backlash on Tuesday, facetiously declaring alongside a childhood Halloween picture that “unfortunately the allegations are true.” In the image, Holscher and her sibling are dressed up as witches, wands at the ready. “I’ve been practicing since elementary school … and I guess my sister has been, too.” Masterson is obviously grasping at straws to dismantle Holscher’s odds. Republicans have recently ramped up spending in the Sunflower State, throwing millions of dollars at Masterson’s campaign to gain an advantage in the governor’s race. As of late last month, the GOP had spent $16.6 million on broadcast and digital expenditures in the race, compared to $4.7 million spent by Democrats, according to the Sunflower State Journal. You can watch the video below. The portion discussing witchcraft starts at the 35:45 mark.
